rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 5-6 report the authors' own design, lab calibration tests (Tables 2-5) and a one-week field test growing spring onions in an acrylic container with a SEN0308 capacitive moisture sensor controlling a solenoid valve.
rows.notes: The study does not report any water savings (no 11% figure, no comparison with a non-sensor or conventional irrigation treatment). It only reports that the automated system applied 0.676 gallons per onion per week (Eq. 2), which is close to a recommended 0.623 gallons (Eq. 4), and concludes the system provides adequate moisture. This demonstrates that the sensor-based system functions and delivers roughly the recommended amount, a precondition for water conservation, not a measured water-saving effect. Single container, one week, no control, no yield or water-use comparison, no dispersion statistics for the claimed effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 5-6 report the authors' own system build, sensor calibration tests and a one-week field test in which onion bulbs were irrigated automatically using the SEN0308 moisture sensor.
rows.notes: The study reports no yield measurement and no 12.05% yield increase. The only crop result is a qualitative observation (Section 6, Figure 18) that after one week spring onions had begun to grow atop a few bulbs and looked healthy. There is no control treatment, no yield quantification, single container, one week. This shows only that the system can keep plants alive/growing (a precondition), not a crop-production gain.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is an engineering demonstration of an ESP32/Blynk drip controller using a SEN0308 capacitive soil moisture sensor; its own quantitative results concern sensor accuracy (Tables 2-4), dripper flow rates (Table 5) and water applied per plant versus a recommended amount. The specific figures in the claim passage (11% water savings, 12.05% yield increase) do not appear anywhere in this study and must originate from the other cited reference.
